newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta seeking to revive sagging economy.
newsitem.headline: Malta seeking to revive sagging economy.

text.p: Malta has started a crash programme to revitalise its economy after three years of slowdown, particularly in its key tourism industry, Prime Minister Alfred Sant said on Thursday.
"The economy over the last two or three years, since the introduction of VAT (Value Added Tax), slowed down, tourism wasn't so good, especially last year," Sant told Reuters.
"So our priority now is...to take out VAT as quickly as possible...and to revive the productive sectors of the economy like tourism."

Tourism is one of the Mediterranean island's main foreign exchange earners and employer for the 370,000 population. But since a record 1994 when 1,176,223 tourists landed, the figures have steadily fallen by five or six percent annually.
Last year, tourism earned around 200 million Maltese pounds ($526 million).
"We believe that this year will not be so good...but by taking steps now to improve the product, next year and the year after that will again be boom years for tourism," Sant said.

Malta was "carrying out infrastructure programmes in major tourism resorts...a crash programme", he said, citing one in Bugibba, on the island's northeastern coast, where 55 percent of all tourists spent some time.
"On the Bugibba project...we will have been spending within three months about three million Maltese lira just to bring the resort into shape."

Foreign consultants are being called in to help make more attractive the island's historical sites -- a plethora of palaces left from the Knights of Malta, walled Arab towns, mediaeval hospitals like that used this week for a Europe and Mediterranean foreign ministers meeting, and the Catholic country's flock of churches from the 16th century.

"We want to make them better accessible, better presented and in an environment which is attractive. We will be spending close to one million plus (Maltese pounds), but that is a slower programme because you can't do crash programmes on historical sites," Sant said.
The government was planning for hotels to open casinos under a franchise from the local casino. "It's a very important tourist attraction," he said.
A new loans system was planned to help modernise industry, particularly for small and medium sized firms, Sant said.

"We are launching a law by which the Malta Development Corporation will back commercial banks to provide finance for these operations and we will be guaranteeing those loans in a way that make it attractive for the small entrepreneur to work.
"We are also providing a new institute to provide technical assistance for these small enterprises."
Sant said he expected that over three to five years a slow start in loans "should pick up in terms of double digit millions".

Elected last October, the Labour government's priority was to "revitalise the economy, rationalise government finances ...and move forward more to the social agenda", particularly education and fighting crime, Sant said.
VAT, introduced by the former Nationalist government as part of its application to join the European Union, will end in summer, the prime minister said.

The tax will be replaced by a "15 percent excise on imports which will come in at an initial stage (and) will gradually be introduced right across the spectrum to affect all local production as well".
The government, which froze the bid to join the EU, wants a "special relationship" with Europe and Sant said he had held talks with European ministers during this week's conference.
He proposed the relationship be based on "deepening" the association agreement which Malta already had with the EU, and talks would continue on this.
($=0.38 Maltese pounds)
